clue.text: Hunt trophy with an old French rifle

parts.note: chasse is the French word for a hunt or the chase
a pot is slang for a cup won as a sporting prize

explanation.surface: A huntsman displays his trophy beside an antique French gun.
explanation.walkthrough: The French theme of the answer lets 'Hunt' be given in French. The chassepot was the French army's breech-loading rifle of the 1860s.
explanation.definitionFit: The chassepot was a bolt-action breech-loader adopted by the French army in 1866, so it is an old French firearm.

clue.text: Funny how hundreds gather round a duck on the motorway

indicators.note: the two letters for hundreds close around the rest, enclosing it

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two of them for hundreds
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so the letter O
the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI

explanation.surface: Something amusing about crowds clustering round a duck that strayed onto a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London to Leeds motorway; its 1 is read as the letter I. 'on' simply puts the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Something comic makes people laugh, which is what funny means.

clue.text: Tune to sing carelessly on excursions

parts.note: an air is a tune or melody

indicators.note: doing something carelessly mixes it up, so the letters of the word are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A melody to be sung casually on day trips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carelessly' rearranges SING into INGS, which follows AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Airings are outings in the open air, short trips taken for fresh air.

clue.text: Spurred by Marines for gulls?

parts.note: imagines riding mounts that belong to the ocean, which marines might spur on as if fooling gulls

explanation.surface: Marine soldiers are spurred on to deceive someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spurred' suggests riding horses, and 'Marines' suggests something belonging to the sea; together they point at the small fish named after horses.
explanation.definitionFit: These small upright fishes have horse-like heads, so they are the steeds of the ocean.

clue.text: Slap-happy toper at the hustings

parts.note: a drinker who loves a wallop, or a big pot of beer, voting at an election

explanation.surface: A punch-drunk boozer turns up at an election meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1832 some English boroughs gave the vote to any householder who boiled his own pot at his own hearth; 'wallop' is also slang for beer and a hard blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A householder who qualified for the parliamentary vote by boiling his own pot on his own fireplace.

clue.text: Death of a German fox

definitions.meaning: a Scots and northern English word for a fox

explanation.surface: A German dies, perhaps killed by a fox.
explanation.definitionFit: It is German for death, and an old dialect name for the fox.

clue.text: Share certificate disallowed the first apostles

definitions.meaning: a provisional document entitling the holder to shares
in Luke, Jesus sends the disciples out telling them to carry neither purse nor a pilgrim's wallet, an old word for such a bag

explanation.surface: A stock certificate is somehow banned from the original twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a financial certificate for shares, and the small satchel the apostles were told not to take with them.

clue.text: Knitted joint for Chips?

parts.note: a neckwear item that is knitted, and also a type of woodworking joint, Chips being the traditional nickname for a carpenter

explanation.surface: A woven link for fried potatoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' is the old naval nickname for a ship's carpenter, who would make a joint by overlapping tapered ends of timber.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a knitted neck covering and a carpenter's joint made by bevelling two timbers to overlap.

clue.text: Premier philosopher

definitions.meaning: Lord John ... was twice British Prime Minister in the nineteenth century
Bertrand ..., the logician and peace campaigner

explanation.surface: A leading thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A family name shared by a Victorian prime minister and his grandson Bertrand, the twentieth-century philosopher.

clue.text: Saints I do knock up, they send up

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Saints I do knock up, they send up (9)' as printed: SAINTSIDO cannot be rearranged to PARODISTS (has N, I where P, R are needed), four letters off, so the fodder is garbled beyond a slip
annotationWithheld.clue: Saints I do knock up, they send up

clue.text: More Dante lessees sound sarcastic

indicators.note: read as 'less E's', so the letter E is removed each time it occurs in the words before it

explanation.surface: Tenants of a Dante text sound cutting and ironic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lessees' is not tenants at all: split it as 'less E's' and drop both Es from MOREDANTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A mordant remark is biting and caustic, the tone of sarcasm.

clue.text: Esteemed man of letters

parts.note: not a writer: the respectful address to a man that opens a formal letter

explanation.surface: A distinguished literary figure is held in high regard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of letters' suggests an author, but the clue means the man addressed at the top of correspondence, with 'Esteemed' giving the affectionate first word.
explanation.definitionFit: The conventional salutation of a formal letter addresses its recipient as a valued gentleman.

clue.text: Anti-energy in Africa

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
go is vigour or energy

explanation.surface: Opposition to energy policy somewhere on the African continent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Congo is a river and two countries in central Africa, so it is something found in Africa.

clue.text: Viaduct vandal

parts.note: a fiend for arches, since a viaduct is a row of arches; the whole is a name for the Devil

explanation.surface: Someone who damages a railway bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whimsically, a fiend attacking a viaduct's arches; in fact the term means Satan, the chief of devils.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief fiend is Satan, the principal enemy of mankind, here pictured as a wrecker of bridges.

clue.text: French and German on this shelf

definitions.text: French and German on this shelf

parts.words: French and German on this shelf
parts.note: French and German people are mainland Europeans, and the seabed fringe around a landmass is a kind of shelf

explanation.surface: Books in French and German are kept on this bookshelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shelf' suggests bookshelves of foreign titles; in fact it is the submerged edge of a landmass.
explanation.definitionFit: Mainland Europeans are described this way, and the shallow undersea margin of a landmass is the shelf of this name.

clue.text: The French would lie to a man

definitions.meaning: the plural definite article in French
add the word lie to these letters and you get Leslie, a man's name

explanation.surface: A Frenchman would tell a fib to another fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: It is French for 'the' before plurals, and it is also the short form of the name Leslie, which is it plus lie.

clue.text: Let gamins somehow become well-connected with these

definitions.text: Let gamins somehow become well-connected with these

indicators.note: the words are put together in some other way, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Street urchins are somehow allowed into good society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges LET GAMINS; read as a whole, bones are joined by these tough bands.
explanation.definitionFit: Ligaments are bands of tissue that bind bones together at joints, keeping the skeleton connected.

clue.text: Unspeakable entertainments

parts.note: not dreadful shows but ones in which nobody can be heard speaking

explanation.surface: Shows so awful they defy description.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unspeakable' usually means appalling; here it is literal: cinema before soundtracks had no spoken dialogue.
explanation.definitionFit: Early cinema had no recorded sound, so its pictures were entertainments without speech.

clue.text: Brainily lean to learning? Far from it

definitions.text: Brainily lean to learning? Far from it

parts.words: Brainily lean to learning? Far from it
parts.note: the opposite of lean is fat, and the opposite of clever is stupid, so a fat head

explanation.surface: Someone inclines cleverly towards study, or perhaps not at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far from it' asks for the opposite of the first half: not lean but fat, and not brainy but dim.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatheaded means stupid, slow-witted, the very reverse of brainy.

clue.text: Suggesting El Greco's palette for the boards?

definitions.text: Suggesting El Greco's palette for the boards?

parts.words: Suggesting El Greco's palette for the boards?
parts.note: El Greco means 'the Greek', so his paint might be 'Greece paint'; the boards are the stage, where actors wear make-up

explanation.surface: Something reminiscent of a Spanish master's colours, for use on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: El Greco was a Greek-born painter, so his colours suggest a pun on Greece; 'the boards' is a traditional term for the theatre stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors put on thick theatrical make-up before treading the boards.

clue.text: Asian farm crossbreed, that's saying?

parts.note: E stands for East or Eastern, the direction of Asia
an imaginary cross between two farm animals, a pig and a ram

explanation.surface: An Eastern hybrid livestock breed — is that what the proverb says?
explanation.walkthrough: The 'crossbreed' is a joke: two farm animals simply side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a short witty remark or maxim, a kind of saying.

clue.text: Island for our 28

definitions.meaning: a Greek island in the Dodecanese, also spelt Kos
28 across begins with salad, and this is a crisp variety of lettuce used in one

explanation.surface: An island that serves our purposes.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the Aegean island off Turkey, and the long-leaved romaine lettuce used in salads.

clue.text: Is able, was active, taking a dramatic part

parts.note: can means is able to
did means acted or performed

explanation.surface: Someone capable and busy who takes a role in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Candida is the title role of Bernard Shaw's 1894 comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Candida is the heroine and title character of a Shaw play, so a role for an actress.

clue.text: Sea power is formidable

definitions.note: the definition is an adjective while the answer is a noun phrase for overwhelming strength

parts.note: the main is an old poetic word for the open sea
force means power or strength

explanation.surface: A navy's strength is impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea power' looks like a single naval idea but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Main force means sheer overwhelming strength, which is what makes something formidable.

clue.text: Finnish young at heart, that is, ardent

indicators.note: the abbreviation is placed in the middle of the word for young fish

parts.note: fry are young fish, with 'Finnish' punning on creatures that have fins
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: A young Finn who is youthful in spirit is passionate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finnish' looks like a nationality but means 'having fins', so the young are fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiery feelings are hot and passionate, just as ardent ones burn.

clue.text: No end of a wrong-doer backed by Fergus

indicators.note: the shortened word is turned round and read from right to left
the final letter of the word for a wrong-doer is dropped

parts.note: a sinner is a wrong-doer

explanation.surface: A villain is supported by an Irishman called Fergus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' removes the last letter of SINNER to leave SINNE, which 'backed' turns round. Fergus is not a man but the river in County Clare on which the town stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennis, county town of Clare in Ireland, stands on the banks of the River Fergus.

clue.text: Despondency at Bridge

parts.note: not gloom at the card table but the Venetian bridge named for prisoners' laments

explanation.surface: A card player is gloomy at the bridge table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' suggests the card game; the Bridge of Sighs in Venice led prisoners to their cells.
explanation.definitionFit: Despondent people breathe out heavily in sorrow, as prisoners did crossing the Venice bridge.

clue.text: Flora here — with her quiverful?

parts.note: a place where young plants are raised, and also a room for a mother's many children, a quiverful being a large family in the Psalms

explanation.surface: Flora is present, together with her large brood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flora' looks like a woman's name but means plants; 'quiverful' recalls Psalm 127, where children are arrows and happy is the man with a full quiver.
explanation.definitionFit: Both young plants and young children are raised in such a place, a garden centre or a children's room.

clue.text: This man's not landed between the trenches

definitions.text: This man's not landed between the trenches

parts.words: This man's not landed between the trenches
parts.note: the ground between the front lines was no man's land; this word is the opposite of no, so it combines with man

explanation.surface: A soldier does not land between the front-line trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: The strip between opposing First World War trenches was called no man's land; replace 'no' with its opposite and you have a sycophant's title.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the affirmative opposite of no, and with man it makes a word for a sycophant.

clue.text: Making Thames-side hay by the ton

definitions.text: Making Thames-side hay by the ton

indicators.note: read as the place minus the word ton: what remains, joined by ton, rebuilds the place name

parts.note: Teddington is a London district on the Thames, site of its tidal lock

explanation.surface: Haymaking on a large scale beside the river Thames.
explanation.walkthrough: TEDDINGTON, a riverside district of south-west London, is the remaining word plus TON, hence 'by the ton'. Tedding is spreading new-mown grass to dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedding is turning and spreading cut grass so it dries into hay, here pictured happening in a Thames-side place.

clue.text: Conversely he's my word of honour

indicators.note: the phrase my word of honour is swapped round so that its two words come in the opposite order

parts.note: 'upon my sam' is an old oath meaning on my word of honour
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man insists, on the contrary, that he is giving his solemn word.
explanation.walkthrough: The oath 'upon my sam' gives the phrase MY SAM; 'Conversely' swaps its words round, making a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common pet form of Samuel, a male name, so it can stand for a man.

clue.text: Green season of show business

definitions.meaning: a time of youthful inexperience, green meaning naive
the title of a long-running 1950s London musical

explanation.surface: A young period spent working in entertainment.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's phrase for one's youthful time of inexperience, also the name of a hit West End musical.
